articles.title: LIVE: Bury Road in Bamford closed as emergency services attend house explosion
articles.excerpt: Bury Road in Bamford is closed from Midgehall Drive to Woodtop Avenue after an explosion at a house at 5.10pm on Tuesday. A witness said her house shook violently.
articles.content_html:
Bury Road in Bamford has been cordoned off after an explosion at a house at 5.10pm on Tuesday 17 November, leaving debris across the road.

The road is closed from Midgehall Drive to Woodtop Avenue.

All emergency services were sent to the scene. Police and the fire service are there now.

A witness, Carol Scott, described it as a suspected gas explosion. The cause has not been confirmed by the emergency services.

Ms Scott said: “Just been an explosion at a house on Bury Road, Bamford, suspected gas explosion. Debris all over Bury Road which is cordoned off. Police and the fire service are at the scene now. Our house shook violently, I thought a plane had landed on us, it was very scary.”

The witness later said the owner of the house was not hurt. She said: “A neighbour went to see the owner and he was uninjured luckily but I think they took him to hosp for a check.”

The emergency services have not yet confirmed any information about injuries.

Rochdale Daily has asked Bamford ward councillors Angela Smith, Stephen Anstee and Phil Beal, and Norden ward councillor Paul Ellison MBE, for comment.

This story will be updated as more information becomes available.

Source: Rochdale Daily newsdesk and witness Carol Scott, 17 November 2026.

The incident occurred during a tense match that ended with York City claiming the title, following the late equaliser from Rochdale. Fans entered the pitch, prompting an investigation by the relevant authorities into the public order charge against Hiram Boateng, who pleaded not guilty.

The match was crucial for both teams, with the outcome affecting their standings in the league. The authorities are currently looking into the circumstances surrounding the pitch invasion and the events that unfolded during the match.

articles.title: Former Clean Air Zone cameras now used by police to fight crime across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Around 400 number plate cameras put up for the scrapped Clean Air Zone have been handed to Greater Manchester Police, with a senior officer saying they have led to multiple arrests.
articles.content_html:
Around 400 number plate cameras installed for Greater Manchester's scrapped Clean Air Zone, which would have covered Rochdale borough roads, are now being used by police to fight crime.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) has taken ownership of the automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras and linked them into its existing ANPR network, according to a Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) report.

Until now, officers could use footage and number plate data from the cameras only after asking permission from Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM), which owned them. The combined authority said that process delayed investigations.

Speaking at Greater Manchester's police, fire and crime panel on Monday 16 November, deputy mayor Kate Green said: "They are not speed cameras, they are being used for crime detection and as an investigative tool."

Deputy Chief Constable Terry Woods told the panel: "I cannot say strongly enough just what a difference that is making."

"It's been tangible, multiple arrests on the back of that system and it's keeping people safe," Mr Woods said, according to the Manchester Evening News.

The cameras were put up across the city region ahead of a charging Clean Air Zone, under which drivers of the most polluting vehicles would have paid up to £60 a day.

The charging scheme was shelved after a backlash. In January 2025 the Government approved Greater Manchester's investment-led Clean Air Plan, which has no charges to drive on local roads.

A six-week public consultation on handing the cameras to police ran from 23 September to 6 November 2025 and drew 4,830 responses.

Of those, 89.7 per cent agreed the cameras' main use should switch to crime detection, while 7.1 per cent disagreed. Rochdale borough residents made up 9.4 per cent of respondents.

Privacy was the most common concern, raised by 38.2 per cent of respondents, followed by data sharing at 37 per cent.

A report to the GM Air Quality Administration Committee in January said 372 Clean Air-funded cameras were operational. The committee decided on 29 January 2026 that GMP would take them over.

GMP is paying the transfer and running costs, according to Clean Air Greater Manchester. TfGM will still receive camera data to monitor the Clean Air Plan, but will not have access to live data.

Greater Manchester remains under a government direction to bring nitrogen dioxide levels on local roads within legal limits in the shortest possible time and by 2026.

Source: Greater Manchester Combined Authority committee report (29 January 2026), Clean Air Greater Manchester, and Manchester Evening News reporting of the Greater Manchester police, fire and crime panel. Photograph: Rochdale Daily image library.

articles.title: Rochdale teenagers born in 2009 or later will never be legally sold tobacco from 1 January
articles.excerpt: The generational smoking ban starts on 1 January 2027, making it an offence to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009.
articles.content_html:
Young people in Rochdale borough born on or after 1 January 2009 will never be legally sold tobacco once the generational smoking ban takes effect on 1 January 2027.

The Department of Health and Social Care began a countdown to the change on Monday 16 November, with a campaign run jointly with the NHS.

From 1 January 2027 it becomes an offence to sell tobacco, herbal smoking products or cigarette papers to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009, under the Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026.

The cut-off does not move. In practice, the legal age for buying tobacco rises by one year every year, so the first group affected, who turn 18 during 2027, will never be able to buy it.

Anyone born before 1 January 2009 can still be sold tobacco as now.

The department described the law as "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to protect future generations from tobacco addiction".

When the bill became law in April, Health Secretary Wes Streeting said: "This legislation marks a turning point for the nation's health."

Shops selling tobacco will have to check whether customers were born on or after 1 January 2009.

They must also display a new notice stating: "It is illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009."

The Act received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026. It also bans advertising and sponsorship of vapes and nicotine products, and gives ministers powers to restrict packaging and displays that appeal to children.

A retail licensing scheme and stronger action against illicit tobacco and vapes are also part of the law, according to the government.

Smoking causes about 80,000 deaths a year in the UK and is the leading preventable cause of death, the government says. There are an estimated 5.3 million smokers in the UK.

Rochdale has a higher smoking rate than England as a whole. Rochdale Borough Council's needs assessment puts it at 15.3 per cent of adults in 2021, against 12.7 per cent nationally.

A YouGov survey in August 2024 found 61 per cent of UK adults supported the ban for those born on or after 1 January 2009, with 27 per cent against.

The ban comes into force on Friday 1 January 2027.

Source: Department of Health and Social Care Facebook post, 16 November 2026; GOV.UK; Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026; Rochdale Borough Council Joint Strategic Needs Assessment. Photograph: UK Government / NHS.

  • Anyone born before 1 January 2009 can still be sold tobacco as now.
  • Shops selling tobacco will have to check whether customers were born on or after 1 January 2009.

articles.title: Heywood homes left without power after cable fault during snow warning
articles.excerpt: Sixty-five properties in north Heywood lost power on Tuesday morning, with engineers aiming to restore supplies by 12.30pm.
articles.content_html:
Sixty-five homes and businesses in north Heywood were left without power on Tuesday morning after an underground cable fault during a snow warning.

SP Electricity North West, which runs the local network, said the properties were hit by an unexpected incident with the underground cable that supplies them.

Engineers were on their way, with a target of restoring power by 12.30pm, according to the operator's incident log reported by the Rochdale Times.

The affected postcodes are OL10 1AA, OL10 1AB, OL10 1AL, OL10 1DT, OL10 1FH, OL10 1FJ, OL10 1FL and OL10 1FN.

Heywood was one of several places hit across Greater Manchester, with almost 500 properties without power at around 7am, according to the operator's figures.

The largest outages were in Saddleworth, where 191 properties were affected, Cadishead and Lower Irlam in Salford, with 126, and Ashton Hurst in Tameside, with 104.

The operator has put the faults down to underground cables and has not said the weather caused them.

It told customers it had no warning before the power went off, and said digging to repair underground cables can make a power cut last longer.

A Met Office yellow warning for snow covered Greater Manchester from midnight until 11am, with forecasters warning of a small chance of power cuts.

The UK Health Security Agency also has a yellow cold-health alert in place for the North West until 9am on Thursday 19 November.

Anyone without power can report it or get updates by calling 105 or 0800 195 4141, which are free from mobiles and landlines.

Residents who need extra help during a power cut, such as those relying on medical equipment, can join the operator's free Extra Care Register.

Source: SP Electricity North West outage information, as reported by the Rochdale Times, BBC North West and Brit Brief; Rochdale Borough Council power cut advice. Image: Rochdale Daily weather graphic.

Among the notable developments, 19-year-old Dan Hackney, who previously played at Warrington, is eager to represent the Hornets again. His return is seen as a significant boost for the team as they prepare for the season ahead.

Lachlan Lanskey has been signed from Keighley, adding depth to the squad. Ongoing contract-extension talks are also in progress with Joe Hickey, indicating the club's commitment to retaining key players as they build a competitive team.

As the Hornets work towards finalising their squad, fans can expect further announcements regarding player signings and contract updates in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Friend backs Springhill Hospice Christmas appeal after Leanne Field’s last Minions party
articles.excerpt: Sally Kerr is backing Springhill Hospice’s Christmas appeal in memory of her best friend Leanne Field, 45, who had one last party at the Rochdale hospice two days before she died.
articles.content_html:
The best friend of a woman who spent her final days at Rochdale’s Springhill Hospice is backing its Christmas appeal in her memory.

Leanne Field, 45, was diagnosed with metastatic sarcoma, a rare type of cancer, in 2021. After time in hospital, she moved into the hospice on Broad Lane at the end of August.

Hospice staff helped her have one last party, surrounded by the people who loved her most, all dressed as Minions, her favourite characters.

The party was held on Saturday 5 September. Leanne died two days later, on Monday 7 September.

Her friend Sally Kerr, 47, of Shaw, who works with Manchester FA, said: “She got admitted to the hospice and originally, it was for symptom management. She’d been in hospital, but it wasn’t the best environment so all we wanted to do was get her in a hospice because I’ve been to hospices before and I have an understanding of what you get, it’s next level and I knew it’d be better for her.”

“We all knew the end was close, but we weren’t ready to say goodbye just yet,” Ms Kerr said.

The pair met in 1998, almost 28 years ago. Ms Kerr said: “I met her at a rave, she loved raving. She danced everywhere, she’d make up a dance to anything. She was just a real character, she was loyal, she was fierce. She was passionate, if you had her love, you had everything. She was just a really good human being.”

Of Leanne’s love of Minions, she said: “She was obsessed she had them all over the house. Everything started going yellow, her tracksuit, trainers, she just loved it. She was a massive kid.”

Ms Kerr said that despite Leanne’s medication and tiredness, her hand began to move when one of her favourite songs was played at the party.

“When one of her songs came on, she was in her wheelchair, and you could just see her revving, and I thought there’s the song, there you go,” she said.

“It meant the world because ultimately, we wanted the opportunity to listen to our music together and to have a little bit of a laugh. You just want that one last time. We wanted Leanne to see that we were still there for her, we wanted her to see she had her girls no matter what.”

Speaking about the hospice, she said: “It’s massive, it’s a big thing. They make it easier and personal, they give you the privacy, and they give you the amenities to spend more time with your loved one. Everything is specific to your loved one in a hospice.”

This will be Ms Kerr’s first Christmas without Leanne. She said: “Without them we wouldn’t have got the memories that we got. It made our last memories with Leanne a little bit better.”

She is urging people across the borough to support the appeal so other families can make similar memories.

“We were all desperate for time with Leanne because your time is not promised. Without the Hospice our last memories would have been going to a hospital. That’s not the environment where we wanted our last memories to be, we wanted her to have the best and be with us,” she said.

Springhill says it is facing increasing demand for its services alongside rising running costs, which have gone up by £2 million in the past five years. The hospice relies on support from the community to keep its services going.

Donations to the Christmas appeal can be made through Springhill Hospice’s website at www.springhill.org.uk/event/christmas-appeal-2026/.

Source: Springhill Hospice press office, press release issued on 16 November 2026. Image: Springhill Hospice / supplied.

articles.title: Seven Sisters to be demolished as RBH plans around 600 new homes at College Bank
articles.excerpt: All seven College Bank tower blocks will come down, with a planning application for around 600 new homes expected in early 2027. RBH expects every remaining customer to have moved out by summer 2027.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks at College Bank are to be demolished and replaced with around 600 new homes, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has decided.

The RBH Board made the decision after more than a year of work with partners in the College Bank Task Force and a review of all available options. RBH will now seek planning approval.

A planning application for the redevelopment is expected to go to Rochdale Borough Council in early 2027. RBH hopes to build a mix of apartment blocks and town houses on the site.

A feasibility study carried out in summer 2025 found that keeping and refurbishing the seven 1960s blocks would cost at least £269 million and take up to 12 years.

RBH said refurbished flats would last around 50 years, while newly built homes are expected to last significantly longer.

Of the 766 flats across the seven blocks, 78 households have yet to accept an offer of a new home. Rehousing will continue, and RBH expects every customer to have moved out by summer 2027.

RBH chief executive Amanda Newton said: "Today marks an important step forward for College Bank and for the future of housing in Rochdale."

She added: "College Bank has been home to generations of Rochdalians, and we recognise the important place the blocks hold in many people's memories."

"This decision gives us a way forward together and allows us to focus on the opportunities ahead," Ms Newton said.

The College Bank Task Force is chaired by the Mayor of Greater Manchester. Its members include the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and Rochdale Borough Council.

Demolition was first proposed in 2017, when RBH warned the blocks were nearing the end of their useful life. Those plans would have taken down four towers, Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow, and refurbished Underwood, Mardyke and Holland Rise.

Tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign in response. They hoped RBH's partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the blocks restored, but that partnership was announced as ending in September 2024.

Residents began moving out in October 2025, after RBH raised concerns about the long-term safety of the blocks. RBH, which has more than 12,000 customers across the borough, says the decision also lets it keep investing in homes elsewhere.

RBH is holding sessions for customers on Wednesday 18 November: at Spotland Community Centre, 92-96 Spotland Road, from 2.30pm to 3.30pm and 4pm to 5pm, and at the Town Mill Brow Community Room, College Bank, from 5.30pm to 6.30pm.

Regular drop-ins continue at the Town Mill Brow Community Room on Tuesdays from 1pm to 4pm and Thursdays from 3pm to 6pm. Residents can also email towncentre.regen@rbh.org.uk or call 0800 027 7769.

Source: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing press office, press release issued on 16 November 2026, with additional reporting by the Local Democracy Reporting Service. Photograph: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing.

articles.title: Kyle Howard pleads guilty to murder of wife Keeley Aspinall in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Kyle Howard, 37, of Tweedale Street, Rochdale, admitted murdering his wife Keeley Aspinall, 44, at Manchester Crown Court and will be sentenced on Wednesday 18 November.
articles.content_html:
Kyle Howard, 37, of Tweedale Street, Rochdale, has pleaded guilty to murdering his wife Keeley Aspinall, 44, whose body was found at their home.

Howard admitted murder at Manchester Crown Court on Monday 16 November, having previously denied the offence, Greater Manchester Police said.

According to police, officers responded at about 4pm on 25 May to a report made by Howard, who said he had killed his wife at their home on Tweedale Street.

Howard told police he had stabbed Ms Aspinall two days earlier and was reporting it because her body was beginning to smell, the force said.

Officers found her body concealed under a bed, and Howard was arrested on suspicion of murder.

As paramedics attended, Howard told them: "There is no point being here, I've done it, she's dead, she's been dead for two days."

After his arrest, Howard spent several days in hospital being treated for an infection to his hand. He was discharged back into police custody on 1 June and charged with murder on 2 June.

Detective Inspector Neil Higginson, the senior investigating officer, said: "Keeley's family have been left devastated by her death and continue to come to terms with the loss of a loved one in the most tragic of circumstances.

"Kyle Howard violently took the life of a woman who should have been safe in her own home. He then concealed Keeley's body beneath a bed and left her there for two days before contacting emergency services."

He added: "Today's guilty plea means Howard has finally accepted responsibility for his actions and has spared Keeley's loved ones the added trauma of having to sit through a lengthy trial."

Howard will be sentenced at Manchester Crown Court on Wednesday 18 November.

articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service has proposed a new fire station in Heywood, set to replace the existing facility on Middleton Road.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service has submitted plans to Rochdale Council for a new fire station in Heywood, aiming to replace the existing facility on Middleton Road with a modern two-storey structure.

If approved, the new station will feature two vehicle bays, accommodation, a community meeting room, a drill yard, and training facilities, including a four-storey training tower.

Crews will operate from a temporary base on the site during construction, which was approved by the council in August 2026.

The design aims to improve safety by allowing fire engines to enter from the rear and exit from the front, reducing the need for reversing onto Middleton Road.

The proposal is part of a wider initiative to upgrade five ageing fire stations across Greater Manchester, including those in Whitefield and Stockport.

Planning documents submitted by Ryder Architecture on behalf of Robertson Construction state that retaining a station on the existing site will maintain excellent service delivery standards for the local community.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: ‘Cruckle’ is the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — an old dialect survival that Rochdale speakers still recognise as a hometown word.
articles.summary: ‘Cruckle’ is the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — an old dialect survival that Rochdale speakers still recognise as a hometown word.
articles.body:
If you’ve ever heard someone in Rochdale say “I cruckled my ankle”, you haven’t misheard an idiosyncratic family coinage. In everyday local use the verb describes that awkward roll or twist of a foot — the sort of stumble you can usually walk off but which leaves you nursing a twinge. Contemporary perceptual-dialect research shows the word is not only used locally but also widely reported by people who explicitly link it to Rochdale speech. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

That research — a 2024 study of folk‑linguistic labels and map‑based perceptions across Greater Manchester — recorded respondents naming “cruckle” among the handful of words they associate with Rochdale when asked to characterise local speech. In the paper’s sample comments the term sits alongside other locally salient items such as guinnel (ginnel) and the label “broad”, which together paint the way people think about where they live and how it sounds. The study therefore gives us two linked facts: cruckle appears in local speech, and people perceive it as a Rochdale marker. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

But the word is not a modern invention. Historical dialect sources trace it to an older northern English verb‑group usually written crookle (and attested in variant spellings), with senses such as “to bend, make crooked, stoop” and extensions to hobbling or walking awkwardly. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect lexicography records crookle in northern and midland counties; linguists treat forms like crookle/cruckle as part of a broader crook/krug family across northern English and Scots dialects. That family’s basic image is simple: a hook‑like or bent motion, frequently expressed with an imitative or frequentative ‑le ending. ([en.wiktionary.org](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Template%3AR%3AEnglish_Dialect_Dictionary/documentation))

The Dictionary of the Scots Language records cognate forms explicitly: kruggle, cruggle and cruckle appear in Scots material with meanings such as “to crouch, bow down, huddle” — semantic cousins of the English crookle senses. Those Scots citations underline two points the dictionaries and comparative work make clear: first, the root is old and part of a northern dialect network; second, similar forms show up in adjacent speech areas (Scotland, northern England, some Scandinavian dialects), so the etymology is regional rather than uniquely local. ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd/kruggle))

So why, if relatives of the word exist elsewhere, does Rochdale feel to many like its home? The answer is social as much as linguistic. Small, recognisable words become local badges when a community keeps using them and when outsiders learn to associate them with a place. Perceptual mapping — asking crowds where they hear particular words — finds exactly that effect: even if related forms exist beyond the borough, concentrated use plus folk awareness make cruckle sound “Rochdale”. The British Library’s dialect collecting work and public callouts have also recorded cruckle/crookle among submissions, which helped confirm its regional currency in living memory. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What does dialect research do with a word like this? Small items are useful evidence. They tell researchers where an older pattern has survived in everyday speech, how people label their own variety, and how social meaning attaches to a single lexical token. For readers of Rochdale, the practical takeaway is straightforward: when somebody says they’ve “cruckled” their ankle, they’re using a durable local verb whose history reaches back into the dialect record, and which functions today as one of the little signals that help people recognise a Rochdale voice. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The training focused on equipping students with skills to advocate for health-related issues, encouraging them to take an active role in improving the wellbeing of their peers and families. This programme is part of a broader effort to engage youth in community health initiatives.

Falinge Park High School has been instrumental in facilitating this training, providing resources and support to ensure students are well-prepared for their roles as advocates. The school aims to foster a sense of responsibility and leadership among its students.

This initiative aligns with ongoing efforts to enhance community health in Rochdale, encouraging young people to contribute positively to their environment. The next steps include further training sessions and opportunities for students to engage with local health projects.
